I was asked last month to look at the yard at the Wellingborough site, where the lorries had been queueing on the access road most afternoons, and where the neighbours had begun to write to the council about the noise and the engines left running for an hour or more at a time. The site manager, who has run the building for nine years and knows every bay in it, told me on the first morning that the problem was the hauliers, who in his view arrived when they liked and expected to be unloaded the moment they pulled in at the gate. I did not think that was the whole story.

When I sat down with the gate log and the booking sheet for the past three months and began to analyse them side by side, it turned out that more than half of the afternoon arrivals had been booked for the afternoon by our own planners, who had been told to keep the mornings free for a large customer whose orders had since moved to another site. Nobody had told the planners that the large customer had gone, so they went on keeping the mornings free for orders that no longer came, and the afternoons went on filling up with lorries that could have been unloaded at nine in the morning without any wait at all. The upshot was a yard that stood half empty until lunch and then filled up so fast that the gate team spent the rest of the day apologising to drivers, to the neighbours and to their own managers, none of whom could see why the numbers looked so bad.

We changed the planning rule that week. The planners now book the first free slot from seven in the morning onwards, the gate team can see the bookings a week ahead on a shared sheet, and any slot left empty by eleven is offered to the hauliers who are already waiting on the road, so that nobody sits there with an engine running for longer than the unloading takes.

I should say that the hauliers were more patient with us than I would have been in their place, and several of them told me that they had stopped bidding for our loads altogether because the waiting cost them more than the work paid, which is a cost that never shows up anywhere on our side of the ledger. Perhaps the most useful thing I did was to stand at the gate for two afternoons with a notebook and write down the time each lorry arrived, the time it reached a door and the time it left, because those three times told me more than three months of reports had managed to tell anyone. That is not a new lesson.

If you manage a yard and the queue on the road is getting longer every week, I would ask you to look first at the rules your own planners follow, and at who last changed them and why, before you write to the hauliers or spend money on a booking system that will only record the same problem in a tidier way. I will go back to Wellingborough in a month to see whether the road is empty in the afternoons and whether the hauliers who left us have started to bid again, and I will write that up for the board with the gate log attached so that anyone can check the times for themselves.
